Name: Liberalism (Classical)
Description: Political philosophy emphasizing individual liberty, limited government, free markets, and rule of law.
CorePrinciples: Individual rights and freedoms as paramount
Limited government constrained by constitution
Free market capitalism
Rule of law and equality before the law
Private property rights
Spontaneous order over central planning
Tolerance and pluralism

Name: Socialism (Democratic)
Description: Political and economic system advocating for social ownership of means of production and democratic control of the economy.
CorePrinciples: Social ownership of means of production
Economic equality and redistribution
Workers' rights and collective bargaining
Universal healthcare, education, and social services
Democratic participation in economic decisions
Critique of capitalism and exploitation
Solidarity and collective welfare over individual profit

Name: Anarchism
Description: Political philosophy advocating for abolition of all hierarchical authority and the state, replaced by voluntary cooperation.
CorePrinciples: Abolition of the state and all coercive hierarchies
Voluntary association and mutual aid
Direct democracy and consensus decision-making
Workers' self-management
Decentralization and federalism
Individual autonomy within community
Critique of all forms of domination

Name: Conservatism (Traditional)
Description: Political philosophy emphasizing preservation of traditional institutions, gradual change, and skepticism of radical reform.
Sources: Reflections on the Revolution in France (Edmund Burke)
CorePrinciples: Tradition and continuity with the past
Gradual, organic change over revolution
Preservation of established institutions
Skepticism of human reason to reshape society
Importance of religion and moral order
Private property and free enterprise
Strong national defense
Respect for authority and hierarchy

Name: Libertarianism
Description: Political philosophy emphasizing maximum individual freedom and minimal government intervention in both personal and economic spheres.
CorePrinciples: Non-aggression principle
Maximum individual liberty in all spheres
Minimal or no government intervention
Free market absolutism
Property rights as fundamental
Voluntary exchange over coercion
Self-ownership
Opposition to taxation as theft

Name: Communitarianism
Description: Political philosophy emphasizing community values, social responsibility, and the common good over individual rights.
Sources: Liberalism and the Limits of Justice (Michael Sandel)
CorePrinciples: Community and social bonds as primary
Common good over individual autonomy
Responsibilities alongside rights
Civic virtue and participation
Shared values and traditions
Critique of excessive individualism
Balance between individual and community

Name: Social Democracy
Description: Political ideology advocating for a capitalist economy regulated to ensure social welfare, labor rights, and reduction of inequality within a democratic framework.
CorePrinciples: Mixed economy: market capitalism with strong state regulation
Universal welfare state: healthcare, education, pensions, unemployment benefits
Progressive taxation to reduce inequality
Strong labor unions and workers' rights
Parliamentary democracy as the path to reform
Social justice without abolishing private property
International cooperation and multilateral institutions

Name: Fascism
Description: Authoritarian ultranationalist ideology emphasizing strong centralized state power, national or ethnic unity, and opposition to liberalism, Marxism, and democracy.
Sources: The Doctrine of Fascism (Mussolini and Gentile)
CorePrinciples: Ultranationalism: the nation or race as supreme organizing principle
Leadership cult: strong authoritarian leader embodies national will
Anti-liberalism and anti-Marxism
Violence and struggle as ennobling and necessary
Glorification of military and war
Corporatist economy: class collaboration under state direction
Social Darwinism: competition between nations and races
Myth of national rebirth and regeneration (palingenesis)

Name: Communism (Marxist-Leninist)
Description: Revolutionary political ideology advocating for the abolition of capitalism and private property, and the establishment of a classless, stateless society through the vanguard party and dictatorship of the proletariat.
CorePrinciples: Abolition of private ownership of means of production
Dictatorship of the proletariat as transitional phase
Vanguard party leads the working class to revolution
Centrally planned economy replaces market
Withering away of the state in final communist stage
Classless, stateless society as ultimate goal
Internationalism: workers of the world unite
Historical materialism: capitalism's contradictions lead inevitably to communism

Name: Nationalism
Description: Political ideology holding that the nation — a people with shared identity, culture, and often ethnicity — should be self-governing and that national interests should take priority.
CorePrinciples: National self-determination: nations should govern themselves
Shared identity: culture, language, history, or ethnicity bind the nation
National sovereignty as paramount value
Priority of national interests over international obligations
Cultural nationalism: preserving and promoting national culture
Ethnic nationalism: membership based on descent (more extreme variant)
Civic nationalism: membership based on shared laws and values

Name: Green Politics / Eco-Socialism
Description: Political ideology integrating environmentalism with social justice, arguing that ecological sustainability requires fundamental transformation of both capitalism and social inequality.
Sources: For the Common Good (Herman Daly and John Cobb)
The Green Case for Socialism (David Pepper)
Green Politics (Fritjof Capra and Charlene Spretnak)
CorePrinciples: Ecological sustainability as foundational political principle
Social justice and environmental justice are inseparable
Capitalism drives ecological destruction; systemic change needed
Degrowth: reducing consumption in wealthy nations is necessary
Renewable energy transition and green economy
Rights of nature and intergenerational responsibility
Participatory democracy and decentralization
Feminism, anti-racism, and environmentalism as interconnected struggles

Name: Populism
Description: Political ideology that pits the virtuous 'people' against a corrupt 'elite,' arguing that politics should express the will of the common people against powerful minorities.
CorePrinciples: Manichean division: virtuous people vs. corrupt elite
Popular sovereignty: the people's will is ultimate political authority
Anti-establishment: existing institutions serve elites, not people
Can be left-wing (economic elite as enemy) or right-wing (cultural elite, immigrants)
Charismatic leader as embodiment of the people's will
Direct democracy and referendums over representative institutions
Crisis narrative: the people are under threat and must act

Name: Christian Democracy
Description: Political ideology applying Christian social teaching to politics, advocating subsidiarity, social solidarity, human dignity, and a regulated market economy within a democratic framework.
CorePrinciples: Human dignity: every person has inherent worth as created by God
Subsidiarity: decisions made at the lowest competent level
Solidarity: mutual responsibility for the common good
Common good over individual or class interest
Family as the fundamental unit of society
Social market economy: capitalism regulated for social justice
Anti-communism and anti-fascism: the third way between extremes
European integration and international cooperation

Name: Feminism (Political)
Description: Political movement and ideology advocating for equal rights, opportunities, and representation for women, and the dismantling of patriarchal structures in society, law, and culture.
Sources: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (Mary Wollstonecraft)
CorePrinciples: Legal and political equality for women (First Wave)
Social and economic equality; challenging domestic roles (Second Wave)
Intersectionality: race, class, and gender oppressions are linked (Third Wave)
Bodily autonomy: reproductive rights as fundamental
Representation: equal participation in politics and institutions
Dismantling systemic patriarchy, not just individual prejudice
Critique of violence against women: domestic violence, sexual assault

Name: Republicanism (Classical)
Description: Political philosophy emphasizing freedom as non-domination, civic virtue, mixed government, and the rule of law to prevent tyranny of individuals or factions.
CorePrinciples: Non-domination: freedom means not being subject to another's arbitrary will
Mixed constitution: balance of monarchical, aristocratic, and democratic elements
Separation of powers to prevent tyranny
Civic virtue: citizens must be active, public-spirited participants
Rule of law: no person above the law
Res publica: politics as the public thing, not private interest
Term limits and rotation of offices prevent concentration of power

Name: Progressivism
Description: Political ideology advocating for social reform, government intervention to address inequality, expanding civil rights, and using policy to achieve positive social change.
Sources: The Promise of American Life (Herbert Croly)
CorePrinciples: Social progress is possible and desirable through collective action
Government has a positive role in addressing social problems
Expansion of civil rights for marginalized groups
Economic regulation to protect workers and the environment
Science and expertise should guide policy
Reform rather than revolution: working within institutions
Universal access to healthcare, education, and economic opportunity

Name: Theocracy / Religious Governance
Description: System of government in which religious authority governs directly or in which law is derived from divine mandate, with clergy or religiously legitimated leaders holding political power.
Sources: Writings of John Calvin on Geneva's theocracy
CorePrinciples: Divine law as the ultimate source of legal authority
Religious leadership holds political legitimacy
No separation of religion and state
Governance as service to God, not just the people
Religious texts as constitutional documents
Duty to implement God's will in the social order
Religious minorities may face restricted rights
Regions: Historical: Geneva, Papal States, Islamic Caliphate
